# T228: an explicit contractive nonlinear SGD model with a positive exact power tail

Version 2, 23 October 2026. Candidate for independent review, not yet a final closure verdict. This revision makes two renewal-theorem conventions explicit; it does not change the theorem or estimates.

This proof addresses the actual T228 registry request for a **concrete nonlinear model**. It does not assert a universal theorem for deep networks. It builds on the existing T228 scalar and radial-tail proofs, especially the forward tilted-walk positivity argument in `rows/T228/claude_b1e26540/T3_STEP3.md`. Those results were already present on 22 October. The additional point here is a fully explicit, nonempty interval with contraction of the actual random nonlinear maps, as the registry asks, rather than only a Foster recurrence condition.

## Model and theorem

Let d=10^{-3}, let s(z)=z+d tanh(z), and take iid pairs (A_k,E_k), each consisting of two independent standard normal variables. The regression teacher is x_*=0, the response is Y_k=E_k, and the sample loss is

    f(x;A,E) = (s(Ax)-E)^2/2.

For every fixed learning rate η in [99/100,101/100], run ordinary, unclipped, constant-step, batch-one SGD

    X_{k+1}=Ψ_k(X_k),
    Ψ(x)=x−η A s'(Ax)(s(Ax)−E).

Then:

1. The random maps are contractive on average. In fact E Lip(Ψ)<q=0.98606303<1.
2. There is exactly one invariant probability law π. Every deterministic initial condition converges to π in Wasserstein distance of order one, geometrically fast.
3. There is exactly one α=α(η)>0 with

       h_η(α):=E|1−η A²|^α=1,

   and 1<α<2. The multiplier is nonarithmetic in logarithmic scale.
4. For some C_η in (0,∞),

       lim_{t→∞} t^α π({x:|x|>t})=C_η.

   The law is symmetric, so each one-sided tail has limit C_η/2. For positive p, its p-th absolute moment is finite exactly when p<α. In particular its second moment is infinite, although the input and label noise have moments of every order.

The constant has the integrable-difference formula

    C_η = E[|Ψ(X)|^α−|(1−η A²)X|^α] /
          (α E[|1−η A²|^α log|1−η A²|]),

where X has law π and is independent of (A,E). The numerator is an expectation of the difference, not a difference of two infinite expectations.

## 1. Bounds on the actual nonlinear update

Put z=Ax, t=tanh(z), and u=sech²(z). Then s'=1+du, s''=−2dut, and

    Ψ'(x)=1−η A² H(z,E),
    H=(1+du)²−2du t(z+d t−E).

The inequalities |t|≤1, 0≤u≤1 and |z|u≤1 imply

    |H−1|≤4d+3d²+2d|E|.

Consequently, with M=1−η A²,

    Lip(Ψ)≤L:=|M|+η A²(4d+3d²+2d|E|).

Also the update is asymptotically linear with a uniform random remainder:

    Ψ(x)=Mx+R(x),
    |R(x)|≤B:=η|A|[d+(1+d)(d+|E|)]   for all real x.

The derivative bound follows from expanding H; the remainder follows from

    s'(z)(s(z)−E)=z+dzu+(1+du)(dt−E).

Both B and L have all positive moments, since they are bounded by polynomials in |A| and |E|. The activation is smooth, nonlinear, and a bounded perturbation of the identity. Its derivative is between 1 and 1+d, and z times either derivative of its perturbation is bounded.

## 2. Explicit average contraction and the tail exponent

For a standard normal A with density φ,

    E|1−A²|=4φ(1)=4/sqrt(2πe)<97/100.

For example, the strict rational bound follows from π>3.14 and e>2.718. The identity follows by splitting at |A|=1, using E(1−A²)=0 and (aφ(a))'=(1−a²)φ(a).

Thus, uniformly over the stated interval,

    E|1−η A²|≤E|1−A²|+|η−1|<98/100.

Using independence, E A²=1 and E|E|<1 gives

    E L < 98/100+(101/100)(6/1000+3/10^6)
         =0.98606303<1.

In particular E log L≤log E L<0 (or this expectation is −∞, which only strengthens the contraction conclusion). Here E|log|M|| is finite: the only finite singularities occur at A=±η^{-1/2}, where they are logarithmically integrable; the Gaussian tails control infinity.

The function h_η(p)=E|M|^p is finite for all p≥0, is strictly log-convex, and has h_η(0)=1 and h_η(1)<1. Gaussian unboundedness gives P(|M|>1)>0, so h_η(p)→∞. Moreover

    h_η(2)=1−2η+3η²≥1.9603>1.

It follows that there is a unique positive root α in (1,2), with h_η(p)<1 for 0<p<α. Its logarithmic derivative at the root

    m_α=E[|M|^α log|M|]

is positive and finite. The positive random variable ξ=|M| has a continuous distribution; log ξ is consequently nonarithmetic. The defining equation is explicit:

    (1/sqrt(2π)) ∫_R |1−η a²|^α exp(−a²/2) da = 1.

For batch size b the same asymptotically linear part is 1−(η/b)χ²_b. The theorem proved here uses b=1; its nonempty interval already supplies the requested nonempty parameter regime.

## 3. Invariant law, uniqueness and lower moments

The Markov operator maps probability laws with finite first moment into themselves because E|Ψ(0)|<∞ and E L<1. Coupling two inputs with the same fresh pair (A,E) contracts their Wasserstein-one distance by at most q. The space of laws with finite first moment is complete for this distance, so the contraction mapping theorem gives a fixed law π and geometric convergence from each deterministic start.

This uniqueness extends to every invariant probability law, without assuming that another invariant law has a first moment. Couple a chain from any finite random initial variable Z with a chain from zero. Then

    |X_n^Z−X_n^0|≤|Z|∏_{j=1}^n L_j→0 almost surely.

Indeed E∏L_j≤q^n, so the product tends to zero almost surely by Markov's inequality and Borel–Cantelli. If the initial law of Z were invariant, bounded Lipschitz test functions and dominated convergence would force it to equal π.

For every 0<p<α, the uniform bound |Ψ(x)|≤ξ|x|+B and h_η(p)<1 give a drift inequality

    E|Ψ(x)|^p≤r_p|x|^p+C_p,   r_p<1.

For p≤1 use subadditivity; for p>1 use (a+b)^p≤(1+ε)a^p+C_{p,ε}b^p and choose ε so that (1+ε)h_η(p)<1. Starting at zero yields a uniform p-moment bound. Weak convergence to π and Fatou's lemma give E_π|X|^p<∞.

The transition kernel has a density bounded below on every pair of compact intervals. To see this, restrict A to [1,2]. Conditional on A=a, Ψ(x) is Gaussian with mean x−η a s'(ax)s(ax) and standard deviation η a s'(ax). For |x|≤R these means and standard deviations stay in a compact set, with standard deviations bounded away from zero. Their densities therefore have a positive common lower bound for |y|≤R. After integrating over a∈[1,2],

    P(x,E_0)≥ε_R Leb(E_0∩[−R,R])  for |x|≤R.

Every interval of positive length consequently has positive π-mass.

## 4. Existence and formula of the exact tail limit

Use the scalar N=1 instance of Jelenković–Olvera-Cravioto, *Implicit Renewal Theory and Power Tails on Trees*, arXiv:1006.3295v5, Theorem 3.1. It is an implicit renewal theorem, not a requirement that the update itself be affine. For R_0=|X| independent of ξ, its hypotheses are: Eξ^α=1, 0<Eξ^αlogξ<∞, logarithmic nonarithmeticity, finite moments of R_0 below α, Eξ^γ<∞ for some 0≤γ<α, and integrability of the weighted discrepancy between the tails of R_0 and ξR_0. Sections 2–3 verify the moment and nonarithmetic hypotheses; γ=0 supplies the extra multiplier moment.

Stationarity and a coupling with the same independent X,(A,E) give

    ∫_0^∞ t^{α−1}|P(|X|>t)−P(ξ|X|>t)|dt
    ≤(1/α) E ||Ψ(X)|^α−|MX|^α|.

The expectation on the right is finite. For 1<α<2, the mean value theorem and |Ψ(X)−MX|≤B bound its integrand by

    c_α[B^α+B ξ^{α−1}|X|^{α−1}].

The first term is integrable, and the second is integrable by independence of X from the step, the lower moment already proved, and the Gaussian moments of B and ξ. The implicit renewal theorem gives a finite nonnegative tail limit and the displayed integrable-difference formula. Strict positivity still requires the following argument.

## 5. Positivity of the tail constant

This section specializes and credits the existing T228 forward-excursion proof. It does not infer positivity merely from the existence of an invariant distribution.

Along a trajectory, let ξ_j=|1−η A_j²| and let B_j be the bound from Section 1. The pairs (ξ_j,B_j) are iid, although their two components need not be independent. With S_n=Σ_{j≤n}logξ_j and V_n=Σ_{j≤n}e^{−S_j}B_j, repeated application of the reverse triangle inequality yields

    |X_n|≥e^{S_n}(|X_0|−V_n).

Tilt the joint one-step law by ξ^α and call the resulting iid law Q. For a stopping time τ and a stopped measurable event F, summing over {τ=n} gives P(F,τ<∞)=E_Q[e^{−αS_τ};F,τ<∞]. No assumption that τ is almost surely finite under P is needed. Under Q, S_n has positive finite drift m_α. For 0<θ<α,

    E_Q e^{−θlogξ}=h_η(α−θ)<1.

Three elementary consequences are needed.

(a) The probability p_+=Q(S_j>0 for every j≥1) is positive. Positive drift makes the future infimum finite almost surely. A finite sequence of increments bounded below by some positive number can first take the walk above a sufficiently large buffer; by independence, with positive probability the remaining walk never exhausts that buffer.

(b) The overshoots O_u=S_{τ_u}−u at τ_u=inf{n:S_n>u} are uniformly tight for u≥0. Here is a direct justification. Chernoff's bound gives

    Σ_{n≥0}Q(S_n≤1)≤e^θ/(1−h_η(α−θ))=:K_U.

By the strong Markov property at the first entry into any interval of length one, its expected total number of visits is at most K_U. Partitioning S_{n−1}≤u into these intervals therefore gives

    sup_{u≥0}Q(O_u>z)≤K_U Σ_{k≥0}Q(logξ>z+k)→0,

because E_Q(logξ)^+ is finite.

(c) V_∞=Σ_{j≥1}e^{−S_j}B_j is finite Q-almost surely. For 0<θ<min(1,α), subadditivity and independence across steps give

    E_Q V_∞^θ≤E[ξ^{α−θ}B^θ]/(1−h_η(α−θ))<∞.

Choose z and then K large enough that

    Q(V_∞>K/2)+sup_u Q(O_u>z)≤p_+/2.

Start the original chain at any y with 2K≤|y|≤4K, and set u=log(t/K), t>4K. The event

    {S_j>0 for j≤τ_u, V_{τ_u}≤K/2, O_u≤z}

is measurable at τ_u and has Q-probability at least p_+/2. On it the chain stays outside [−K,K] until it exceeds t. Changing measure gives a uniform lower bound

    P_y(hit {|x|>t} before [−K,K])
       ≥(p_+/2)e^{−αz}(K/t)^α.

The compact minorization in Section 3 gives a uniformly positive chance from [−K,K] to reach the annulus {2K≤|y|≤4K} in one step. Finally, stationarity gives the last-exit inequality

    π(D)≥∫_A π(dx) P_x(τ_D<τ_A^+),

for disjoint A,D, where τ_A^+ is the first strictly positive return time. For completeness, split {X_N∈D} by the last visit to A among times 0,…,N−1; the resulting events are disjoint. Stationarity converts their sum to the expected number of visits to D before the first return to A, which dominates the probability of any such visit. Let N increase.

Apply this with A=[−K,K] and D={|x|>t}. Since π(A)>0, the preceding estimates imply π(D)≥c t^{−α} with c>0. Combined with Section 4, this proves C_η>0.

## 6. One-sided tails and exact moment threshold

Oddness of s and evenness of s' imply Ψ_{A,−E}(−x)=−Ψ_{A,E}(x). The noise law is symmetric, so reflecting an invariant law produces another invariant law. Uniqueness therefore makes π symmetric and splits the absolute tail equally between its signs. The positive power-tail limit makes every moment of order p≥α infinite by the tail-integral formula; Section 3 gives finiteness below α.

## Scope, attribution, and literature boundary

The registry requests an example, rather than a theorem for every neural-network loss. This example is a genuinely nonlinear single neuron, with the requested Gaussian input, persistent Gaussian labels, unchanged constant-step SGD, actual average contraction, nonarithmetic asymptotically linear multiplier, explicit positive tail law, and α<2 throughout a nonempty learning-rate interval.

Existing Math Brain T228 proofs establish substantially more than this scalar example under their stated stability assumptions. This document consolidates their mechanism and supplies an explicit contraction regime so that closing the concrete-model request does not rely on silently weakening average contraction to recurrence. No discovery credit is reassigned.

Primary background: Gürbüzbalaban–Şimşekli–Zhu, *The Heavy-Tail Phenomenon in SGD*, arXiv:2006.04740; Jelenković–Olvera-Cravioto, arXiv:1006.3295v5, Theorem 3.1. The recent Li–Lei–Wei–Wu paper arXiv:2610.23750v1 assumes regularly varying innovations and studies a vanishing-step regime. The model here has Gaussian one-step data and a fixed step, so that paper does not directly supply this theorem. A search that finds no identical theorem is not a proof of novelty.

# T228: an explicit nonlinear SGD model with a nonzero teacher

Version 1, 23 October 2026. A09 extension and verification.

Source candidate: `campaign/proofs/T228_EXPLICIT_CLOSURE.md`, Version 1,
SHA256 `9d0ef065e10642dbc8967870bdc3f368300424659f9316456355775264133287`.
This document proves the extension rather than assuming that the zero-teacher
symmetry or input-label independence survives. It retains the existing T228
forward-excursion positivity mechanism, credited in Section 10.

## 1. Model and theorem

Fix

```text
δ = 1/1000,  σ(z) = z + δ tanh(z),
θ ∈ [−1,1],  η ∈ [99/100,101/100],  b = 1.
```

Let `(A_k,E_k)` be iid pairs of independent standard normal variables, set
`Y_k = σ(A_k θ) + E_k`, and use the unmodified squared sample loss and SGD map

```text
fθ(x;A,E) = (σ(Ax) − σ(Aθ) − E)²/2,
Ψθ(x) = x − η A σ'(Ax)(σ(Ax) − Y),
X_(k+1) = Ψθ,k(X_k).
```

The parameters are fixed along a trajectory. The labels are not independent of
the inputs when `θ ≠ 0`.

**Theorem.** For every such fixed `(η,θ)`:

1. The actual smooth random maps satisfy

   ```text
   E Lip(Ψθ) < q := 99010707/100000000 = 0.99010707 < 1.
   ```

   In particular they contract on average, including in the logarithmic sense.
   The maps are nonaffine almost surely.
2. There is exactly one invariant probability `π_(η,θ)`, including among laws
   without an assumed first moment. It has a finite first moment and, for every
   deterministic initial point `x`,

   ```text
   W₁(Law(X_n^x), π_(η,θ)) ≤ q^n W₁(δ_x, π_(η,θ)).
   ```

   Its support is all of `R`.
3. There is a unique positive solution `α = α(η)` of

   ```text
   hη(α) := E|1−ηA²|^α = 1,
   ```

   and `1 < α < 2`. The exponent is independent of the teacher `θ`.
4. There is a finite strictly positive constant `C_(η,θ)` such that

   ```text
   lim_(t→∞) t^α π_(η,θ)({x: |x|>t}) = C_(η,θ) ∈ (0,∞).
   ```

   The same limit and constant hold with `|x−θ|` in place of `|x|`. For `p>0`,
   both the `p`th absolute moment and the `p`th absolute estimation-error moment
   are finite exactly when `p<α`. Their second moments are infinite.

With `X∼π_(η,θ)` independent of the fresh pair `(A,E)`, the constant is

```text
C_(η,θ) = E[|Ψθ(X)|^α − |(1−ηA²)X|^α] /
          (α E[|1−ηA²|^α log|1−ηA²|]).                         (1)
```

The expectation in the numerator is an absolutely integrable coupled
difference. It is not a subtraction of two separately finite expectations.

For `θ=0`, the invariant law is symmetric and each one-sided tail has constant
`C_(η,0)/2`. **No one-sided tail limit or equality of one-sided constants is
asserted here for a fixed nonzero teacher.** In fact the stationary law for a
nonzero teacher is not symmetric about zero; Section 9 proves this directly.

The concrete choice `θ=1, η=1` is a nonzero-signal example covered by the
theorem. The contraction bound is uniform on the stated rectangle; no uniform
lower bound on `C_(η,θ)` is claimed.

## 2. Actual derivative, label dependence, and uniform remainder

Write `z=Ax`, `t=tanh(z)`, and `u=sech²(z)`. Then

```text
σ'(z)=1+δu,   σ''(z)=−2δut,
Ψθ'(x)=1−ηA² H(z,Y),
H(z,Y)=(1+δu)²−2δut(z+δt−Y).
```

Since `|t|≤1`, `0≤u≤1`, and `|z|u≤1`, expansion gives

```text
|H−1|
≤ 2δu + δ²u² + 2δ|z|u|t| + 2δ²u t² + 2δu|t||Y|
≤ 4δ + 3δ² + 2δ|Y|.
```

For example, `|z|u≤1` follows from
`cosh²(z)=1+sinh²(z)≥1+z²≥|z|`. Consequently, with

```text
M=1−ηA²,  ξ=|M|,
Lθ=ξ+ηA²(4δ+3δ²+2δ|Y|),
```

the mean value theorem on the whole real line yields

```text
Lip(Ψθ) ≤ Lθ.                                                  (2)
```

This is a bound on the actual global Lipschitz constant of the nonlinear map.
It is not merely a bound on its asymptotic multiplier.

The changed mixed label moment must keep the dependence between `A` and `Y`.
Using `|tanh v|≤|v|`,

```text
|Y| ≤ (1+δ)|θ||A| + |E|,
E[A²|Y|]
≤ (1+δ)|θ| E|A|³ + E[A²|E|]
= (1+δ)|θ|·2√(2/π) + √(2/π)
≤ (3+2δ)√(2/π) < 3+2δ = 3.002.                               (3)
```

Only the second summand uses independence, namely independence of `A` and
the additive noise `E`. No factorization of `E[A²|Y|]` is made.

For the remainder, the exact identity

```text
σ'(z)(σ(z)−Y)=z+δzu+(1+δu)(δt−Y)
```

implies

```text
Ψθ(x)=Mx+Rθ(x),
sup_(x∈R)|Rθ(x)| ≤ Bθ := η|A|[δ+(1+δ)(δ+|Y|)].                (4)
```

In particular, uniformly on the parameter rectangle,

```text
Bθ ≤ (101/100)|A|[δ+(1+δ)(δ+(1+δ)|A|+|E|)].
```

Both `Bθ` and `Lθ` have moments of every positive order. Their envelopes are
polynomials in `|A|` and `|E|`; the same is true of the label envelope. Neither
`Bθ` nor `Y` needs to be independent of `M`.

The sample map is genuinely nonlinear. At zero its derivative is
`1−ηA²(1+δ)²`, whereas its derivative tends to `1−ηA²` as `|x|→∞`
whenever `A≠0`; the terms containing `u` or `zu` vanish. These two values
differ for every `A≠0`, an event of probability one.

## 3. Exact contraction arithmetic and the exponent

Let `φ` be the standard normal density. Splitting at `|A|=1`, and using
`(aφ(a))'=(1−a²)φ(a)`, gives

```text
E|1−A²| = 4φ(1) = 4/√(2πe) < 97/100.
```

This strict inequality needs no quadrature: `π>157/50` and `e>1359/500`
give

```text
(97/100)² · 2(157/50)(1359/500) − 16
= 7532467/125000000 > 0.
```

The pointwise inequality
`|1−ηA²|≤|1−A²|+|η−1|A²` now yields `Eξ<98/100`.
Combining this with (2)–(3) and `EA²=1`,

```text
E Lip(Ψθ) ≤ E Lθ
< 98/100 + (101/100)[4/1000 + 3/10^6 + (2/1000)(1501/500)]
= 98/100 + (101/100)(10007/10^6)
= 99010707/10^8
= 0.99010707 < 1.                                             (5)
```

The margin is exactly `1−q=989293/10^8=0.00989293`. Jensen gives
`E log Lip(Ψθ)≤log E Lip(Ψθ)<log q<0`, with an extended negative
expectation also sufficient. The envelope itself has a finite negative log
expectation: putting `c₀=4δ+3δ²<1`, one has
`Lθ≥|1−ηA²|+c₀ηA²≥c₀`, while `log⁺Lθ≤Lθ`.

The distribution of `M=1−ηA²` is absolutely continuous. Its only zeros as a
function of `A` are `±η^(−1/2)`, where the derivative is nonzero. Hence

```text
P(ξ=0)=0,
E|log ξ|<∞,
E[ξ^p |log ξ|]<∞  for every p>0.
```

Local logarithmic integrability proves the assertions near the two roots;
Gaussian decay proves them at infinity. The law of `log ξ` is absolutely
continuous and thus nonarithmetic. Jensen also gives
`E log ξ≤log Eξ<0`.

The function `hη(p)=Eξ^p` is finite for all `p≥0`, has strictly convex
logarithm, and satisfies

```text
hη(0)=1,   hη(1)<0.98<1,
hη(2)=1−2η+3η² ≥ 1−2(99/100)+3(99/100)²
                    =19603/10000=1.9603>1.
```

The last inequality uses that the polynomial is increasing on the chosen
interval. Moreover `P(ξ>1)>0`, so `hη(p)→∞` as `p→∞`.
Strict log-convexity gives exactly one positive root `α∈(1,2)`, with
`hη(p)<1` for `0<p<α`. Its tilted logarithmic mean

```text
mα := E[ξ^α log ξ]
```

is finite and positive. Positivity follows, for example, by comparing the
derivative of `log hη` at `α` to its strictly positive secant slope from
`p=1` to `p=α`. All these quantities depend on `η` and not on `θ`.

## 4. Invariance, uniqueness, convergence, and lower moments

At zero,

```text
Ψθ(0)=η(1+δ)A Y,
E|Ψθ(0)|<∞.
```

Fresh-step coupling and (5) contract Wasserstein distance of order one by
at most `q`. The Markov operator maps the complete space of probability
laws with finite first moment into itself. The contraction mapping theorem
therefore supplies an invariant law `π=π_(η,θ)` in that space and the
displayed geometric convergence bound.

To remove a possible hidden moment restriction from uniqueness, couple a
chain from any finite random initial value `Z` with a chain from zero, using
the same independent fresh steps. Then

```text
|X_n^Z−X_n^0| ≤ |Z| ∏_(j=1)^n Lθ,j → 0  almost surely.
```

Indeed the expectation of the product is `(ELθ)^n≤q^n`; Markov's inequality
and Borel–Cantelli show that the product tends to zero. If `Z` had any
invariant probability law, bounded Lipschitz test functions and dominated
convergence would identify it with `π`. No moment of `Z` is used.

For every `0<p<α`, (4) gives a moment drift. For `p≤1`,

```text
E|Ψθ(x)|^p ≤ hη(p)|x|^p + E Bθ^p.
```

For `p>1`, use
`(a+b)^p≤(1+ε)a^p+C_(p,ε)b^p`, choosing `ε>0` so that
`r_p=(1+ε)hη(p)<1`. Thus in both cases

```text
E|Ψθ(x)|^p ≤ r_p |x|^p + d_p,    r_p<1, d_p<∞.
```

The chain started from zero has uniformly bounded `p`th moments. Its weak
convergence to `π` and the lower semicontinuity of `|x|^p` imply
`Eπ|X|^p<∞`.

## 5. Changed conditional mean and explicit compact minorization

Conditional on `A=a`, the fresh additive noise remains standard normal and

```text
Ψθ(x) = μθ(x,a) + η a σ'(ax) E,
μθ(x,a)=x−η a σ'(ax)[σ(ax)−σ(aθ)].                            (6)
```

This conditional mean includes the teacher term. For `a∈[1,2]`, `|x|≤R`,
and all permitted parameters, its absolute value is at most

```text
D_R := R + 4(101/100)(1+δ)²(R+1),
```

because `|σ(v)|≤(1+δ)|v|`. The conditional standard deviation is in

```text
[s_min,s_max] := [99/100, 2(101/100)(1+δ)].
```

For any finite `R,T>0`, the conditional density at every `|y|≤T` is
therefore at least

```text
d_(R,T) := [s_max√(2π)]^(-1)
           exp(−(T+D_R)²/(2s_min²)) > 0.
```

After integrating over `a∈[1,2]`, with
`ε_(R,T):=P(1≤A≤2)d_(R,T)>0`, one obtains

```text
Pθ(x,F) ≥ ε_(R,T) Leb(F∩[−T,T]),   |x|≤R.                    (7)
```

In particular every nonempty open interval has positive transition
probability from every point. Stationarity then gives it positive `π` mass.
The support of `π` is the whole real line. This check also supplies the
uniform compact-to-annulus transition used in the positivity proof.

## 6. Exact absolute-tail limit and its integrable-difference formula

Use Jelenković–Olvera-Cravioto, *Implicit Renewal Theory and Power Tails on
Trees*, [arXiv:1006.3295v5](https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.3295v5), Theorem 3.1,
printed page 5 of the [primary PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1006.3295).
Its `N=1` specialization applies to `R₀=|X|`, `C₁=ξ`, independent by

```text
≤ α Bθ(W+Bθ)^(α−1)
≤ α[Bθ^α + Bθ ξ^(α−1)|X|^(α−1)].                            (8)
```

## 7. Strict positivity with the nonzero-teacher joint coefficient law

All the bounds below use `Bθ` from (4), including its teacher-dependent
label. The full steps `(A_j,E_j)` are iid, so their images `(ξ_j,Bθ,j)`
are iid. Within a pair the two components can be dependent. In this scalar
model no rotation argument or teacher symmetry is used to obtain iid pairs.

### 7.1. Forward radial inequality and joint tilt

Put

```text
S₀=0,  S_n=Σ_(j=1)^n log ξ_j,
V_n=Σ_(j=1)^n exp(−S_j)Bθ,j.
```

Repeated reverse triangle inequalities give, pathwise,

```text
|X_n| ≥ exp(S_n)(|X₀|−V_n).                                  (9)
```

Tilt the law of each complete step by `ξ^α` and call the iid product law
`Q`. This is a probability law because `Eξ^α=1`. On the first `n` complete
steps its density relative to the original law `P` is `exp(αS_n)`.
For a stopping time `τ` and a stopped event `F`, summing over `{τ=n}` gives

```text
P(F,τ<∞)=E_Q[exp(−αS_τ) 1_{F,τ<∞}].                         (10)
```

No infinite-path absolute continuity or uniform-integrability claim is
needed. Under `Q`, the increment `Z=log ξ` satisfies
`E_Q|Z|<∞`, `E_QZ=mα>0`. Thus `S_n→∞` almost surely under `Q`.

Fix `β=1/2`. Since `1<α<2`,

```text
r := E_Q exp(−βZ)=hη(α−β)<1.                                 (11)
```

### 7.2. A positive survival probability

The process `exp(−βS_n)` is a nonnegative supermartingale under `Q`.
Stopping at the first time an independent walk reaches `(-∞,−1]`, truncated
at time `n`, gives

```text
Q(inf_(n≥0) S_n ≤ −1) ≤ exp(−β).
```

Because `Q(Z>1)>0`, a first increment above one followed by a fresh walk
that never reaches `−1` proves

```text
p₊ := Q(S_j>0 for every j≥1)
≥ p₀ := Q(Z>1)(1−exp(−β)) > 0.                              (12)
```

The event `Z>1` has positive probability because the Gaussian input is
unbounded and the tilt has a strictly positive density where `ξ>0`.

### 7.3. Uniformly tight overshoots

Let `τ_u=inf{n≥1:S_n>u}` for `u≥0` and `O_u=S_(τ_u)−u`.
The positive drift makes `τ_u` finite `Q`-almost surely. Chernoff's bound
and (11) give

```text
Σ_(n≥0) Q(S_n≤1) ≤ K_U := exp(β)/(1−r).
```

If `I=(a,a+1]` and `ν_I` is its first entry time, then, conditional on
`S_(ν_I)∈I`, a later visit to `I` entails a fresh-walk displacement at most
one. The strong Markov property therefore gives the translated occupation
bound

```text
U(I):=Σ_(n≥0)Q(S_n∈I)≤K_U.
```

Partitioning `(-∞,u]` into `(u−k−1,u−k]`, and dropping the restriction of
no earlier crossing, now gives, for `z≥0`,

```text
Q(O_u>z)
≤ Σ_(n≥1) E_Q[1_{S_(n−1)≤u} Q(Z>u+z−S_(n−1))]
≤ K_U Σ_(k≥0)Q(Z>z+k)
≤ K_U[Q(Z>z)+∫_z∞Q(Z>v)dv] → 0.                            (13)
```

The final bound is independent of `u` and tends to zero because `E_QZ⁺`
is finite.

### 7.4. Summable discounted teacher-dependent remainders

Using subadditivity at exponent `β=1/2` and then independence of a step
from its past,

```text
E_Q[(Σ_(j≥1)e^(−S_j)Bθ,j)^β]
≤ Σ_(j≥1) r^(j−1) E_Q[ξ^(−β)Bθ^β]
= E_P[ξ^(α−β)Bθ^β]/(1−hη(α−β)) < ∞.                        (14)
```

The numerator is the correct joint moment. It is finite because `α−β>0`
and both factors have all positive polynomial moments under `P`; there is
no inverse-multiplier singularity. Thus
`V_∞=Σ_(j≥1)e^(−S_j)Bθ,j<∞` almost surely under `Q`.

### 7.5. Excursions and the finite-stopping-time likelihood ratio

Choose `z≥0` so that the supremum in (13) is at most `p₀/4`, then choose
`K≥1` so that `Q(V_∞>K/2)≤p₀/4`. These choices are made before the
tail threshold `t`.

For `t>4K`, set `u=log(t/K)` and use the stopped event

```text
F_u={τ_u<∞, S_j>0 for 1≤j≤τ_u, V_(τ_u)≤K/2, O_u≤z}.
```

The union bound, (12), and the two preceding choices show
`Q(F_u)≥p₀/2`. On this event, for every initial point with
`2K≤|y|≤4K`, (9) implies

```text
|X_j| ≥ (3K/2)e^(S_j)>K  for 1≤j≤τ_u,
|X_(τ_u)| > (3K/2)(t/K) > t.
```

Thus it forces a hit of `D_t={|x|>t}` before the central interval
`C=[−K,K]`. On `F_u`, `S_(τ_u)≤u+z`. Equation (10) consequently gives

```text
inf_(2K≤|y|≤4K) P_y(τ_(D_t)<τ_C)
≥ (p₀/2)e^(−αz)(K/t)^α.                                    (15)
```

The hitting times in (15) start at time one; the initial annulus lies
outside both sets. Under `P`, `τ_u` need not be almost surely finite;
equation (10) already restricts to its finite-crossing event.

### 7.6. Stationary last-exit transfer

For disjoint Borel sets `C,D`, let `τ_C^+=inf{n≥1:X_n∈C}`. In a
stationary chain, the events specifying the last visit to `C` before time
`N`, among paths with `X_N∈D`, are disjoint. Consequently

```text
π(D)
≥ ∫_C π(dx) Σ_(j=1)^N P_x(X_j∈D, j<τ_C^+)
→ ∫_C π(dx) E_x[Σ_(j≥1)1_{X_j∈D,j<τ_C^+}]
≥ ∫_C π(dx) P_x(τ_D<τ_C^+).                                 (16)
```

The limit uses monotone convergence. This is an unnormalized stationary
integral; no return-time or regeneration factor is omitted.

Take `C=[−K,K]` and `J={2K≤|y|≤4K}`. Equation (7) with `R=K,T=4K`
gives

```text
inf_(x∈C) Pθ(x,J) ≥ δ_K := 4K ε_(K,4K)>0.
```

The Markov property at the first step, followed by (15), gives for `x∈C`

```text
P_x(τ_(D_t)<τ_C^+)
≥ δ_K(p₀/2)e^(−αz)K^α t^(−α).
```

Full support yields `π(C)>0`. Applying (16) therefore proves

```text
π(D_t) ≥ c_(η,θ) t^(−α),
c_(η,θ):=π(C)δ_K(p₀/2)e^(−αz)K^α>0,  t>4K.
```

Together with Section 6, this establishes `C_(η,θ)≥c_(η,θ)>0`.

## 8. Exact moment threshold and the nonzero-signal example

For a nonnegative random variable `R` and `p>0`,
`ER^p=p∫₀∞t^(p−1)P(R>t)dt`. The strictly positive tail limit makes
the integral diverge for every `p≥α`; Section 4 proves finiteness below
`α`. A bounded translation preserves the limit, since for `t>|θ|`,

```text
P(|X|>t+|θ|) ≤ P(|X−θ|>t) ≤ P(|X|>t−|θ|).
```

Thus the same constant and moment threshold describe estimation error.

For the explicit nonzero teacher `θ=1`, the labels are
`Y=A+δ tanh(A)+E`. They contain a nonconstant input-dependent signal, with

```text
E[AY]=1+δ E[A tanh(A)]>1.
```

More generally the population risk has the unique minimizer `θ`:

```text
Fθ(x)=E fθ(x;A,E)
     =1/2+(1/2)E[σ(Ax)−σ(Aθ)]²
     ≥1/2+(1/2)(x−θ)².
```

The inequality uses `σ'≥1` and `EA²=1`, and equality at `x=θ` proves
uniqueness of the minimizer. Thus `θ=1` is a genuine nonzero regression
teacher, not a renamed zero-signal model.

At the concrete learning rate `η=1`, the same exact arithmetic sharpens

```text

h₁(1)=4/√(2πe)<0.97,  h₁(2)=2.
```

`t^(−α(1))`, where `α(1)∈(1,2)` is the unique solution of

## 9. What symmetry does and does not survive

The exact reflection identity is

```text
Ψ_(−θ,A,−E)(−x)=−Ψ_(θ,A,E)(x).
```

Because the additive noise is symmetric and the invariant law is unique,
`π_(η,−θ)` is the reflection of `π_(η,θ)`. At `θ=0` this makes one law
symmetric and gives both one-sided constants `C_(η,0)/2`. It also gives
`C_(η,−θ)=C_(η,θ)` for the absolute tails. At fixed `θ≠0`, reflection
changes the model parameter; it is not a symmetry of that model.

One can even rule out exact symmetry about zero when `θ≠0`. Stationarity
and the finite first moment imply

```text
0=E[A σ'(AX)(σ(AX)−σ(Aθ))],                                 (17)
```

after averaging out the fresh mean-zero additive noise. Both terms are
integrable by `σ'≤1+δ`, `|σ(v)|≤(1+δ)|v|`, and `Eπ|X|<∞`.
If `π` were symmetric, the expectation of
`A σ'(AX)σ(AX)` would be zero, because its integrand is odd in `X` for
each fixed `A`. The other term
`A σ'(AX)σ(Aθ)` has the strict sign of `θ` almost surely when `A≠0`.
This contradicts (17). Thus the nonzero-teacher invariant law is not
symmetric about zero. Equal asymptotic one-sided constants would require
a separate signed-tail argument and are not inferred here from the
absolute-tail theorem.

```text

≤ α[B^α + B ξ^(α−1)|X|^(α−1)].
```


The inclusion is true because every point of I is at most one above s. Summing over m≥0 and then over σ yields


## 6. Discounted error with the dependence preserved

The reverse-triangle recursion gives, by induction,


For 0<θ<min(1,α), apply subadditivity to finite partial sums of V and then monotone convergence. For each j≥1, independence is used between step j and its **past**, not between ξ_j and B_j:

```text

= E_Q[e^(−θS_(j−1))] E_Q[ξ_j^(−θ) B_j^θ]
= r_θ^(j−1) E_P[ξ^(α−θ)B^θ].
```

```text

≤ E_P[ξ^(α−θ)B^θ] Σ_{j≥1}r_θ^(j−1)
```




## 8. Stationary last-exit inequality: explicit finite-horizon proof

This is the most consequential potential source of a direction or normalization error. The candidate's direction and normalization are both correct.

Let the chain be stationary, let A and D be disjoint Borel sets, and put τ_A⁺=inf{n≥1:X_n∈A}. For a fixed N≥1, the following N events are disjoint, indexed by k=0,…,N−1:

```text

```

They are the possible last visits to A before the endpoint, among paths ending in D. Paths that have no visit to A in the window supply a nonnegative remainder. Therefore stationarity and the Markov property give

```text
π(D)
≥ Σ_{k=0}^{N−1} P_π(E_(k,N))
= ∫_A π(dx) Σ_{j=1}^N P_x(X_j∈D, τ_A⁺>j)
= ∫_A π(dx) E_x[Σ_{j=1}^N 1{X_j∈D, j<τ_A⁺}].
```

```text

≥ ∫_A π(dx) E_x[Σ_{j=1}^{τ_A⁺−1}1{X_j∈D}]
≥ ∫_A π(dx) P_x(τ_D<τ_A⁺).
```

```text
≥ δ_K (p₊/2)e^(−αz)K^α t^(−α),  x∈A.
```

## 3. Stationarity, uniqueness, moments, and support

The Markov operator is a contraction on the complete space of probability laws with finite first moment. The finite moment of `Psi(0)` is immediate from `Psi(0)=eta(1+d)AE`. Banach's theorem yields the invariant law and the geometric Wasserstein-one convergence of the law from every deterministic start.

The extension to uniqueness among all invariant probability measures is sound. One may choose any proposed stationary initial variable independently of future samples. The iid Lipschitz bounds give `E product L_j <= q^n`; Markov's inequality and Borel-Cantelli force that product to zero almost surely. Multiplication by any finite initial difference preserves this convergence, even when the initial law has no first moment. Bounded Lipschitz test functions then identify its stationary law with the constructed one.

The moment drift uses `E xi^p<1`, not `E L^p<1`; that distinction is correct because the uniform affine remainder bound is available. The inequalities for the cases `p<=1` and `p>1` give a genuine coefficient below one, without any factorization of `xi` and `B`. The passage from uniformly bounded moments to the limiting law follows from lower semicontinuity/Portmanteau, equivalently a suitable Fatou argument.

The compact minorization is valid: conditioning on `A in [1,2]` gives a normal transition with bounded mean and a standard deviation bounded above and away from zero when the starting point lies in a compact interval. Its density has a positive infimum over the required compact sets. Every nonempty interval therefore has positive invariant mass. In particular, the compact set used in the final excursion argument has positive mass, and an annulus at a fixed finite distance can be reached uniformly from it in one step.

## 5. Adversarial check of the positive-constant proof

### The joint tilt and stopping time

For fixed eta and its root alpha, the one-step tilted probability is

\[
dQ(a,e)=|1-\eta a^2|^\alpha\,dP(a,e).
\]

It is normalized because `h(alpha)=1`. Taking iid steps preserves independence across time and preserves the actual within-step dependence between `xi` and `B`. The full joint law may be used, or its pushforward to `(xi,B)`; the path event used in the proof is measurable from these pairs and the pathwise lower bound holds for every full sample realization.

For a stopped event `F`, summation over `{tau=n}` gives

\[
P(F,\tau<\infty)
=\sum_{n\ge1}E_Q[e^{-\alpha S_n};F,\tau=n].
\]

This is the correct argument even though the hitting time can be infinite under `P`. It does not invoke an unjustified optional-stopping equality or uniform integrability of the likelihood martingale. Under `Q`, the positive drift makes the level-hitting time finite almost surely. Version 2 states this stopped change-of-measure convention correctly.

### Positive survival probability and tight overshoots

Positive finite drift gives an almost surely finite future minimum. There is a positive-probability finite run of increments bounded below by some positive number. An independent future walk stays above the negative of a sufficiently large accumulated buffer with positive probability. This proves `p_+>0`, including the requirement of strict positivity at each preceding step.

The overshoot estimate also works. Write `Y=log xi` and `rho=E_Q exp(-theta Y)=h(alpha-theta)<1`. Chernoff gives

\[
\sum_{n\ge0}Q(S_n\le1)\le e^\theta/(1-\rho)=K_U.
\]

For an arbitrary interval of length one, stop at its first entrance. Starting anywhere inside that interval, every later visit implies that the subsequent increment sum is at most one. Strong Markov therefore bounds the expected total visits by `K_U`, uniformly over the interval's location.

Partition the positions immediately before a crossing of level `u` into `(u-k-1,u-k]`. An overshoot above `z` from such a position requires the fresh increment to exceed `z+k`. Independence of this increment from the past, followed by the uniform visit bound, yields the displayed sum. It is permissible to drop the first-crossing restriction in this upper bound. The sum tends to zero because `E_Q Y^+<infinity`. This is a real proof of uniform tightness, not a renewal-theoretic assertion assumed without hypotheses.

### Discounted errors and absence of hidden independence

The essential factorization is

\[
E_Q[e^{-\theta S_j}B_j^\theta]
=\rho^{j-1}E[\xi^{\alpha-\theta}B^\theta].
\]

Only the previous steps are factored from the current **joint** pair. The same-step `xi_j` and `B_j` remain inside one expectation. Since `0<theta<min(1,alpha)`, the coefficient exponent `alpha-theta` is positive and the mixed moment is finite. Summing and using subadditivity proves `E_Q V_infinity^theta<infinity`. There is no substitution of `E_Q B^theta E_Q xi^(-theta)`.

Choose the overshoot cutoff and the error cutoff so the sum of the two bad-event probabilities is at most `p_+/2`. A union bound then gives the good stopped event probability at least `p_+/2`; independence of survival, overshoot, and accumulated error is neither available nor needed.

For `2K<=|y|<=4K`, on that event all intermediate times have

\[
|X_j|\ge e^{S_j}(2K-K/2)>K,
\]

and the final time has `|X_tau|>(3/2)t>t`. The bounded overshoot supplies the lower bound on the stopped likelihood. Thus the claimed uniform excursion hitting probability proportional to `t^(-alpha)` is valid.

### Conversion to a stationary tail

The one-step annulus entrance uses the original compact minorization. Future samples are fresh after that entrance, so the uniform bound over entrance points applies by the Markov property.

The last-exit inequality is correct and does not require reversing time or assuming independent excursions. For every `N`, disjoint last-visit events give

\[
\pi(D)\ge\sum_{k=1}^N
\int_A\pi(dx)P_x(X_k\in D,\tau_A^+>k).
\]

Letting `N` increase gives the expected number of visits to `D` before return, which dominates the probability of at least one such visit. In combination with the compact mass and annulus entrance probability, this proves a strictly positive `liminf t^alpha pi(|x|>t)`. The finite limit established in Section 4 must therefore be strictly positive.

## 1. Exact substitution and independence

\[
M=1-\eta A^2,\qquad \xi=|M|,\qquad

Thus \(R_0\) is independent of \(\xi\). Independent future copies can be appended on a product space if one follows the tree proof literally.

The stationary output \(U=|\Psi(X)|\) is a coupled variable with the same marginal law as \(R_0\). The application does **not** claim that \(U\) is independent of the current \(\xi\); this generally fails and is unnecessary. Independence is imposed on the input \(R_0\).

## 3. Lower moments precede renewal

\[
|\Psi(x)-Mx|\le B,\qquad

This proves the needed moments without tail regular variation, a finite \(\alpha\)-moment, or a positive tail constant. Existence of \(\pi\) uses the earlier average Lipschitz contraction and finite first moment of \(\Psi(0)\).

## 4. Absolute discrepancy: no critical moment is needed

Put \(U=|\Psi(X)|\), \(V=|MX|=\xi|X|\). Stationarity gives \(U\overset d=R_0\), while \(|U-V|\le B\). Pointwise indicator comparison and Tonelli give

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\int_0^\infty t^{\alpha-1}
|\mathbb P(R_0>t)-\mathbb P(\xi R_0>t)|\,dt\\
&\qquad\le
\mathbb E\int_0^\infty t^{\alpha-1}
|\mathbf1_{\{U>t\}}-\mathbf1_{\{V>t\}}|\,dt
=\frac1\alpha\mathbb E|U^\alpha-V^\alpha|.
\end{aligned}
\]

There is no subtraction of divergent integrals. Since \(0<\alpha-1<1\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
|U^\alpha-V^\alpha|
&\le\alpha |U-V|\max(U,V)^{\alpha-1}\\
&\le\alpha B(V+B)^{\alpha-1}\\
&\le\alpha B\xi^{\alpha-1}|X|^{\alpha-1}+\alpha B^\alpha.
\end{aligned}
\]

The second term is integrable. For the first, independence of the stationary input from the step gives

\[
\mathbb E[B\xi^{\alpha-1}|X|^{\alpha-1}]
=\mathbb E[B\xi^{\alpha-1}]\,\mathbb E|X|^{\alpha-1}<\infty.
\]

Indeed \(\xi^{\alpha-1}\le1+\xi\), and \(\mathbb E[B(1+\xi)]<\infty\) by Gaussian polynomial moments. Correlation of \(B\) and \(\xi\) is allowed. The state moment was established above; for this discrepancy alone, even the finite first moment from contraction suffices.

Thus the full absolute discrepancy integral is finite, including both improper endpoints, before renewal is invoked.

## 5. Formula and signed-to-radial reduction

The same absolute integrability permits Fubini for the signed difference:

\[
\int_0^\infty t^{\alpha-1}
\{\mathbb P(R_0>t)-\mathbb P(\xi R_0>t)\}\,dt
=\frac1\alpha\mathbb E[U^\alpha-V^\alpha].
\]

Consequently the constant is exactly

\[
C_\eta=
\frac{\mathbb E[|\Psi(X)|^\alpha-|MX|^\alpha]}
{\alpha\,\mathbb E[\xi^\alpha\log\xi]}.
\]

The bracketed difference is integrable. Neither individual power is asserted integrable. Splitting its expectation into two expectations would be invalid after positivity is proved; the candidate expressly avoids that operation.
